clue.text: Farewell, O Duke of Milan!

parts.note: to fare well is to thrive or do well, which is to prosper

explanation.surface: A theatrical goodbye addressed to a ducal ruler of Milan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Farewell' reads as a goodbye, but split it: fare well, to do well. The rightful Duke of Milan is the magician in Shakespeare's The Tempest.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's The Tempest the exiled magician is the usurped ruler of that Italian city.

clue.text: Models have their problems

explanation.surface: Fashion models have their troubles too.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who sit for artists are sitters who pose, and tricky questions or puzzles are also so called.

clue.text: With which to prevail at Lord's ?

definitions.text: With which to prevail at Lord's ?

parts.words: With which to prevail at Lord's ?
parts.note: Lord's is the London cricket ground, so read the word as the power of an over, a set of six balls bowled

explanation.surface: Asking what it takes to win at the home of cricket, or in the House of Lords.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord's is the London cricket ground; an 'over' is a cricket bowling spell of six balls, so the strength of an over is how one prevails there.
explanation.definitionFit: To prevail is to overcome or subdue, and split the word gives cricket's over plus strength.

clue.text: Recipes made up exactly right

indicators.note: made up means put together, so the letters of the word before are assembled anew

explanation.surface: Recipes that have been prepared exactly as written.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made up' rearranges the letters of RECIPES.
explanation.definitionFit: Something accurate and exact is spot on, correct in every detail.

clue.text: They alleviate that sinking feeling

parts.note: 'that sinking feeling' is dismay, but here literal sinking into water, which floating platforms prevent

explanation.surface: Things that cheer one up when despondent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That sinking feeling' is an idiom for dread; here it is a literal sinking, stopped by floating log platforms.
explanation.definitionFit: Floating platforms of logs or planks keep people from sinking in water.

clue.text: Pain which will in time save more?'

definitions.text: which will in time save more

explanation.surface: Some ache that might, if handled promptly, spare further trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition plays on the proverb 'a stitch in time saves nine': the clue coyly says 'more' for nine.
explanation.definitionFit: A sharp side-ache while running has this name, and the proverb says a timely sewing repair prevents nine more.

clue.text: Without a clue he'd have been fair mazed

definitions.text: Without a clue he'd have been fair mazed

parts.words: Without a clue he'd have been fair mazed
parts.note: a 'clue' or clew was originally a ball of thread, which Ariadne gave the Greek hero to find his way out of the Labyrinth

explanation.surface: Someone who would have been utterly bewildered without a hint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clue' comes from clew, a ball of thread; 'fair mazed' is dialect for completely amazed and a nod to the Minotaur's labyrinth.
explanation.definitionFit: The Athenian hero who killed the Minotaur escaped the Labyrinth only by following Ariadne's thread.

clue.text: It is not, commonly speaking, pollution

explanation.surface: Someone denying, in casual speech, that something counts as pollution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Commonly speaking' signals a colloquial contraction: 'tain't is dialect for 'it ain't', it is not.
explanation.definitionFit: Dialect shortens 'it ain't' to a contraction, and contamination or corruption is a blemish of the same spelling.

clue.text: A bit of a swine, with a capacity for drink

explanation.surface: A rather nasty person who can hold a lot of alcohol.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A bit of a swine' sounds like a mild insult; it is literally a pig's head.
explanation.definitionFit: A pig's head is part of a swine, and a large cask holding about 54 gallons of ale or wine bears the same name.

clue.text: Cross in a strange state of stupefaction

indicators.note: strange means odd, so the letters of the preceding words are put in an odd order

explanation.surface: Someone angry and in a peculiarly dazed condition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strange' rearranges CROSS IN A; 'Cross' looks like an adjective meaning angry but is only fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Stupor induced by drugs, or by nitrogen in deep diving, is a narcotic daze.

clue.text: What a relief when it ended in 1900!

definitions.text: What a relief when it ended in 1900!

parts.words: What a relief when it ended in 1900!
parts.note: 'relief' is not just comfort but the military relief of a besieged South African town during the Boer War, lifted in May 1900

explanation.surface: A sigh of gratitude that some ordeal finished at the turn of the century.
explanation.walkthrough: The relief of the besieged town in May 1900 caused wild celebrations in Britain; 'relief' is the military term for lifting a siege.
explanation.definitionFit: The Boer War encirclement of a South African town held by Baden-Powell was broken in 1900, an event known as its relief.

clue.text: Work unsuited to a mendicant ?

parts.note: split 'mendicant' as 'mend I can't': a beggar announces he cannot do mending jobs

explanation.surface: A beggar is not the person to hire for a job.
explanation.walkthrough: A mendicant is a beggar, but read the word as 'mend-I-can't' and he is the last person to give fixing-up jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: Mending and fixing jobs are this kind of work, which someone saying 'mend I can't' would refuse.

clue.text: Sounds a deceitful beast

indicators.note: tells us the word is chosen for how it is spoken, not how it is spelt

parts.note: a deceitful person is a cheater

explanation.surface: A complaint that some animal is crafty and dishonest.
explanation.walkthrough: In British speech, which drops the final R, 'cheater' is said the same as the big cat's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The fastest land animal is a spotted big cat, so a beast.

clue.text: Plucky little nippers

parts.note: 'plucky' means made for plucking (eyebrows) and 'nippers' are small pincers, not brave children

explanation.surface: Brave young children.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nippers' is British slang for small children and 'plucky' for brave; here they are small gripping tools used for plucking hairs.
explanation.definitionFit: Small pincer tools are used to pluck hairs, so they are little nipping instruments that pluck.

clue.text: He used to qualify as one

definitions.text: He used to qualify as one

parts.words: He used to qualify as one
parts.note: 'used' means took on staff rather than formerly: someone who uses workers counts as their boss

explanation.surface: A man who was once qualified for something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Used to' reads as 'formerly'; here it means 'he who used (staff)', which qualifies a person as one who hires.
explanation.definitionFit: To employ is to use people's labour, so whoever uses workers is their boss.

clue.text: A pie's uncommonly brown

indicators.note: uncommonly suggests the letters are arranged in an unusual way

explanation.surface: A remark that a pie has baked to an unusually brown colour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uncommonly' rearranges the letters of A PIE'S, the apostrophe ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a reddish-brown pigment from cuttlefish ink, the tint of old photographs.

clue.text: Concert for 19.?

parts.note: 19 is the people who take things in their stride, and a Prom concert is named after a walk or stroll, fit for them

explanation.surface: Asking what concert suits the solver of entry 19.
explanation.walkthrough: A Prom is a concert where people stand or stroll; the full word also means a walk, fitting for 19's walkers.
explanation.definitionFit: A Prom concert takes its name from this word, which also means a seafront walk where strollers go.

clue.text: The drug a girl mixed

indicators.note: mixed means jumbled, so the letters before it are stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: A young woman blending a drug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mixed' rearranges THE DRUG A.
explanation.definitionFit: A female child of her parents is a girl in relation to them.

clue.text: Longfellow's was airborne-destination unknown

parts.note: 'I shot ... into the air, It fell to earth, I knew not where'

explanation.surface: A poet's flight, whose landing place nobody knew.
explanation.walkthrough: The poem begins 'I shot an arrow into the air, It fell to earth, I knew not where', hence airborne with no known destination.
explanation.definitionFit: The projectile shot in the poet's famous lines flew into the sky and landed nobody knew where.

clue.text: They take things in their stride

definitions.text: They take things in their stride

parts.words: They take things in their stride
parts.note: the idiom means coping calmly, but read literally it is people moving by strides

explanation.surface: Calm people who cope with anything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take things in their stride' means cope calmly; literally, it describes people on foot.
explanation.definitionFit: Pedestrians and hikers move by striding, so they literally go at a stride.

clue.text: Labour out of work ? What a situation!

definitions.text: Labour out of work ? What a situation!

parts.words: Labour out of work ? What a situation!
parts.note: the political party Labour out of office is in a state of ...; the word for such a state is also a job and a situation

explanation.surface: Exclaiming at unemployment, or at the Labour Party out of government.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'situation' is an old word for a job, and a party out of office is in a certain political place; both are covered by one word.
explanation.definitionFit: A job is called a post or situation, and a state of affairs is also a stance or place, matching both.

clue.text: Used solely by machine-operators ?

parts.note: 'solely' means with the sole of the foot, not exclusively: a foot pedal driving a sewing machine or lathe

explanation.surface: Something reserved exclusively for people who run machines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Solely' reads as 'only'; split it as worked by the soles of the feet, a foot pedal for an old sewing machine or lathe.
explanation.definitionFit: A foot-operated lever drives old sewing machines and lathes, worked by the sole.

clue.text: Members of Poe's household

parts.note: points to Poe's tale 'The Fall of the House of ...', whose family members are Roderick and Madeline

explanation.surface: The servants or relatives who lived with Edgar Allan Poe.
explanation.walkthrough: Not Poe's own household: the House of Usher in his tale, whose family name in the plural also means those who show people to seats.
explanation.definitionFit: Poe's story concerns the doomed House of Usher, so its members bear that name; doormen showing guests to seats share it.

clue.text: Supporter of World Revolution forced to recant

definitions.text: Supporter of World Revolution forced to recant

parts.words: Supporter of World Revolution forced to recant
parts.note: not a communist revolutionary but the astronomer who backed the idea that the Earth revolves round the Sun and was made by the Inquisition to retract it

explanation.surface: A believer in global communist revolution made to renounce his views.
explanation.walkthrough: 'World Revolution' sounds political; it is the Earth's revolution round the Sun, which the Italian astronomer upheld until the Church forced him to recant in 1633.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian astronomer championed the Copernican view of a moving Earth and was compelled by the Inquisition to abjure it.

clue.text: Cyril bursts into song

indicators.note: bursts suggests something broken apart, so the letters of the name are scattered and regrouped

explanation.surface: A man named Cyril suddenly starts singing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bursts' rearranges CYRIL; 'into' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The words of a song, or a short song-like poem, are called by this term.

clue.text: Jackets designed for smokers?

explanation.surface: Coats tailored for people who smoke, like a smoking jacket.
explanation.walkthrough: Smoking jackets exist, which is the trap: the second sense is cannabis cigarettes, which are made to be smoked.
explanation.definitionFit: A double-breasted sailor's coat is a reefer jacket, and slang names a cannabis cigarette a reefer.

clue.text: This elephant, however, does forget — to behave !

definitions.text: This elephant, however, does forget — to behave !

parts.words: This elephant, however, does forget — to behave !
parts.note: plays on the saying that an elephant never forgets: a solitary wild bull elephant is the exception, forgetting its manners

explanation.surface: An elephant that, against the proverb, forgets something.
explanation.walkthrough: Elephants 'never forget', but the dash shows what this one forgets: how to behave. A dangerous lone elephant is given this name.
explanation.definitionFit: A violent elephant living apart from the herd is called this, a word also for a badly behaved person.

clue.text: People are bound to run in it

definitions.text: People are bound to run in it

parts.words: People are bound to run in it
parts.note: 'bound' means tied together, not certain: pairs run with a leg of each tied to the other

explanation.surface: An event that everyone is sure to take part in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound to' reads as 'certain to'; here it means tied, as at a school sports day where partners run with adjacent legs strapped together.
explanation.definitionFit: This sports-day event pairs runners with two of their legs tied together, so they are literally bound as they run.

clue.text: Wherein the rest of the business takes place ?

definitions.text: Wherein the rest of the business takes place ?

parts.words: Wherein the rest of the business takes place ?
parts.note: 'the rest' is not the remainder but a break from business, as when Parliament or a court stops sitting

explanation.surface: A query about where the remaining items on an agenda are handled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The rest of the business' looks like the remaining agenda; it is the rest taken from business, a break in sittings.
explanation.definitionFit: A suspension of Parliament or court sittings is a break, a rest from business.

clue.text: It's not their fault that they are hare-brained

definitions.text: It's not their fault that they are hare-brained

parts.words: It's not their fault that they are hare-brained
parts.note: 'hare-brained' means foolish, but these creatures really do have the brains of a hare, being young ones

explanation.surface: Excusing people who act rashly and foolishly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hare-brained' means reckless; read literally, a young hare can only have a hare's brain.
explanation.definitionFit: Young hares in their first year have this name, and naturally have a hare's brain.
